old_title: South Africa v Australia: third men's cricket Test, day one - live
new_title: Starc strikes back as Australia dismiss South Africa for 329 on day one of third Test - as it happened
old_text:
38th over: South Africa 185-1 (Markram 72, Bedingham 15) Back to Lyon then, the lone wicket-taker. Over the wicket to Markram, giving it lots of air, looking to draw a mistake. "Two and three, boys," is the mantra from Carey, trying to keep spirits up. Those spirits currently have a lot of headroom.
37th over: South Africa 182-1 (Markram 70, Bedingham 14) Starc needs to find something: some lift, some bounce. He does get a ball to rear at Markram, but Markram is able to play it down behind point for one. Bedingham mistimes a pull shot, and it does pop up, but lands in a gap on the leg side. Wasn't really short enough, he was on it too early and it took a top edge near the toe of the bat. Australia desperately need one of these mis-hits, of which there have been a few, to fall their way. Not a bad over, in the end, but still five singles from it. And wait... a no ball. "Sorry, sorry," says Dick Illingworth for the late notice, as the players were drifting away. And the extra costs him! Bedingham back-cuts him for four! Down through deep third.
36th over: South Africa 172-1 (Markram 67, Bedingham 8) Simon Katich is very critical on commentary about Australia leaving out Boland, which is interesting, because Katich is not one to throw around big opinions for their own sake. He says that it sends the wrong message to everyone to leave out your best player from the previous Test. He says that you have to back performance. There is a case to be made that way.
Gorgeous straight drive from Bedingham. A session of pain lies behind them, but a day of pain looms for Australia. The batter repeats the dose from Hazlewood, but a touch wider this time and finds mid off.
35th over: South Africa 167-1 (Markram 66, Bedingham 4) Starc comes back, and smoked through point by Markram! That's his 800th run against Australia, in 14 hits. His average is back over 60 against this lot, in live terms. A little drive adds run 801.
34th over: South Africa 162-1 (Markram 61, Bedingham 4) Hazlewood immediately comes on to bowl to Bedingham, who has fallen to pace in each innings thise series. Some nice defensive shapes from Bedingham, who then expands into a cover drive for four.
Paul O'Neill writes in. "Re: Matthew Doherty's post (and your response). The two precedents to this flying start by SA (Edgbaston 2005 and Brisbane 2002) were very different, to my mind. I feel that Ponting put England in as an aggressive move - looking to press home the 1-0 series advantage - but I suspect that Nasser just didn't want to expose his batting lineup to yet more trauma at the hands of McGrath, Warne, etc. So which camp does Cummins fall into?"
Good question. I don't think he has huge faith in his batting, especially without Smith, but if they were ever going to bat well, it's day one in bright sunshine. Head and Renshaw would have enjoyed this track. I think the Aussies just got duped by the idea of more moisture in the wicket early. Cummins has been a bowl-first captain, much more than most. He's always considering it as a tactic, even on the days when he doesn't go that way.
33rd over: South Africa 158-1 (Markram 61, Bedingham 0) Suddenly the tempo changes. With Cummins to Markram, there are no streaky pull shots. Markram does nail one drive, but straight back at the bowler, preserving his own face by collecting that on the bounce. Otherwise, Markram waits and watches.
32nd over: South Africa 158-1 (Markram 61, Bedingham 0) It's been a bit of a wait, but Lyon has Test wicket 574. South Africa, notwithstanding, have an incredible platform. Markram and Ackerman don't quite get the Luckhurst-Boycott record.
WICKET! Ackerman st Carey b Lyon 95, South Africa 157-1
Falls short of a hundred! Ohhh, the frustration. Ackerman half smiles, half grimaces as he walks off. Well into the 90s, wants to keep the foot down, stay true to the style that has brought him here. Charges down at Lyon, and the old stager is wise to that trigger movement, that foot shuffle that gives the batter away. Very slow and very wide - not Lyon, but the ball he bowls, sending it way outside the off stump, Ackerman moving to the leg side, and realising too late that he won't be able to reach it. He tries desperately to get any sliver of bat on that ball, but can't, and Carey's work is routine.
31st over: South Africa 157-0 (Markram 60, Ackerman 95) Another close call for Ackerman, that same pull shot! Goes at Cummins, gloves it in the air, and again it goes so fine, just past the keeper, away to the fence.
29th over: South Africa 148-0 (Markram 58, Ackerman 88) Cummins taking responsibility, but Ackerman keeps taking him on. Another heaving pull shot, another single to fine leg. He doesn't look convincing playing those, they never come out of the middle of the bat, and the top edge may do for him eventually. He'll probably have a ton by then, though!
28th over: South Africa 144-0 (Markram 57, Ackerman 85) Second ball after lunch, and it's another dropped catch! Lyon is excellent off his own bowling, has been his whole career, but this one is absolutely hammered, Ackerman charging and smoking it, but it was almost straight at Lyon, no need for a dive, just had to position the hands to absorb the impact. He can't, and the ball ricochets away, through Hazlewood at mid off, who almost makes a hash of his chase back to the rope. Just manages to keep the scoring to two, does the tall fast bowler. Nothing is going right for Australia.
"Marques Ackerman has now scored more in one innings (58) than Maddinson in four (56). Food for thought..." writes Luca Human.
Genuinely one of the worst Australian selection decisions ever made: for the team, for the wellbeing of the player, and for the integrity of the domestic system. I have a feeling that repercussions will continue for a long time.
This came in just before the break from Etienne Terblanche. "On the cusp of lunch...is anyone thinking of Barry Richards at Kingsmead in 1970. Incomparable, obviously, but 94* or thereabouts would be quite a feat from the young fella who looked as stodgy as Fred Swarbrook last week..."
Indeed, Richards was mentioned on commentary: he got to 94 and then blocked the last over to be responsible! A ton in the first session is wildly rare in Test cricket, only six players have done it to my recollection.
Ackerman had reason for stodge last week, to be fair. Zaltzman tells me that in first-class games since June 2025, he averages 70 and strikes at 99.
"Is Scott Boland the best reserve pace bowler ever?" asks Ewan Glenton. "What is it, he's played 20 tests over about five years and has nearly 90 wickets at 18.5? It brings to mind Malcolm Marshall when he carried the drinks for two or three years, kept out by Roberts, Holding, Garner & Croft, but Marshall was very young at the time and people generally didn't know how good he was or would become. But Boland... it's as if, say, the Windies also had a world-class spinner so peak Colin Croft kept on getting squeezed out."
I like the comparison. He does have an astonishing record, 87 wickets at 18.44. I have every hope that he'll get to 100 over the next few months. The thing is, if he were playing instead of Hazlewood, as people seem to suggest most often, then Hazlewood would also be the best reserve bowler over, with 311 wickets at 23.
Here's an email on this theme from Rob Knap. "I realise this already looks like a 'we'll have a bowl' gone wrong in the historical way. A different bowler in the Aussie attack probably wouldn't make a big difference... but: Scott Boland. The three quicks in the Big Four always seem to play if fit. Starc's not been great this series (as I type this Ackerman is smacking him all over the park). But then I suppose Starc bolsters the batting in a way Boland doesn't. But surely Boland should be playing, however they squeeze him in?"
This debate has been had a lot, so I'll lay out the case for the defence. Imagine three more career wickets for Hazlewood, and all four of Australia's bowling attack will be in the top seven Australian wicket-takers of all time.
Currently it goes Hazlewood, Johnson, Cummins, Lillee, Starc, McGrath, Lyon, Warne.
That's pretty bloody handy.
Boland has an incredible record, absolutely. And then Hazlewood in the last three years has 67 wickets at 15. Starc was player of the series in the Ashes last summer, which at times he seemed to be playing almost single-handed. Cummins is probably the best of the lot.
Starc has had a middling two Tests matches. He also has 450 wickets, and has literally got better every year of his career so far. Cricket is a highly variable sport. Performances jump all over the place. Someone not having an impact in one game doesn't mean, when you're at the selection table, that their next one will be poor. It's about how much you rate their ability to possibly have a good game. The best players have a higher possibility rating, a greater likelihood that they will play well.
Australia have five excellent bowling options, and can pick four. That's all it is. Whoever was left out, there would be a strong case that they should play. You can say 'How could they not pick x' about everyone. It's as simple as that.
Doesn't mean they haven't bowled badly today. But that's another matter.
Eamonn Maloney, your sentiment will be widely echoed. Of course, no knowing whether he would have done any better, or been slotted off his length to damage those beautiful career figures.
On that prior stat, I can add that there are also opening partnerships of 162 and 165 against Australia in matches when they've chosen to bowl first, but those were in the third innings, not the first. Atherton-Butcher in 1997, and Gavaskar-Chauhan in 1981.
Another great stat from Andy Zaltzman - this is what happens when he doesn't have a BBC call to work for.
In a first innings when Australian teams have sent in an opponent, this is already the second-highest opening stand. Brian Luckhurst and Geoff Boycott put on 171 during the first WACA match in 1970, so today's pair have 31 runs to go. Might knock that off in five overs after lunch.
Lunch - South Africa 140 without loss after being sent in
After being sent in! Gooooodness me. Pat Cummins will carry the can for this, but surely it was a coach-captain-senior-player decision. I can't imagine that he just made the call himself walking to the toss. But it has gone horribly, horribly wrong.
Three things. One, conditions. Sunshine and nothing in the surface, no swing, no seam, no turn. Easy.
Two, Australia. They've bowled poorly, even in the conditions. A lot of short balls, a lot of width, a lot down the leg side. That has allowed so many of the shots we've seen.
Three, South Africa. Both players have made the most of the things going in their favour. Markram gave one chance against the run of play, Ackerman had a couple of false strokes, but they were good enough to really go after what they could go after, and middled a lot of deliveries.
27th over: South Africa 140-0 (Markram 56, Ackerman 82) Cummins to close it out before the break, and Markram drops and dashes a single. Ackerman does the same, not going to do anything silly at this stage of the session. Last ball, Markram edges through a vacant slip for four, and that puts a very appropriate full stop on an absolute disaster of a session for Australia. The South African leave the field walking on air.
26th over: South Africa 134-0 (Markram 51, Ackerman 81) Commentary is talking about an Ackerman hundred before lunch, but Markram is taking the strike and charging to fifty instead. He cuts Lyon for four, then produces that back-foot punch again for another. He averages fifty-plus against Australia, and here he is again. Then he pinches the strike!
25th over: South Africa 125-0 (Markram 42, Ackerman 81) The smashathon continues! Lunch not far away, and Starc still bowling indifferently, short and wide and slashed away by Ackerman. Next ball, arrows in at the pads, and Ackerman is ready for that! Cleans it out over midwicket for four more. Third ball? Same result, nothing wrong with the deliver this time, just outside the off stump, but Ackerman trusts the bowler's pace, opens the face, and guides it over the slips. Again, shots you can't play elsewhere, but we haven't seen a single ball move laterally off the surface.
Fourth ball? Four more! Uppercut again, this time much squarer. The last one went over the gap between first and second slip, this one over gully, but Ackerman is trusting his ability to guide the ball anywhere.
Finally, from the fifth ball, he has to defend. Drops the ball at his feet. And Markram is still aware enough to pinch the single. Then keeps strike. 18 from the over.
I'm having flashbacks to Shikhar Dhawan on debut against Australia. A ton off... was it 89 balls? Someone can look that up. Ackerman isn't quite on debut, but the next best thing.
24th over: South Africa 107-0 (Markram 41, Ackerman 64) Lyon continuing, and the singles flow freely. Everyone is asking about bowling first. Surely, having brought your spinner back and having kept your left-armer to make the footmarks outside the right-hander's off stump, you would want to give him the chance to bowl last, not to be operating before lunch?
Gervase Greene emails in. "Seeing Baz Boland as drinks waiter, again, is a bit confronting. I do get why he was surplus to the situation in this case - it looking like a solid batting wicket and all that. But boy does that then beg the question 'why the hell did we send them in...?' Only a cynic might suggest we needed another 24 hours to sort out our batting order. (24 weeks might be better...)"
23rd over: South Africa 103-0 (Markram 40, Ackerman 62) This is a team falling apart in real time. Travis Head drops Markram, one of the easiest catches you will ever see at Test level. Just wasn't paying attention.
Markram tries to drive another length ball, misreads the bounce, gets it up near the splice. The ball doesn't loop up, it goes relatively flat but gently and slowly to cover, where Head is placed. He doesn't seem to see it, because he jumps as the ball reaches him, as if thinking that it has been smashed. It hasn't, but Head with both feet off the ground and his hands all over the place is in no position to hold it, and instead parries it away. Can't get it on the rebound either. The body language there strongly suggests that he'd drifted off, and was surprised to see a ball coming at him.
22nd over: South Africa 102-0 (Markram 39, Ackerman 62) Markram pulls, and for a second Cummins thinks that he's in the game, the uncontrolled top edge swirling away, but there's a big gap behind square with the possible catcher set much finer, and the ball lands safely for a run. Markram didn't know where it went either. But no such ambiguity around Ackerman's shot, as he follows up with another fine hook for six! Every time he plays the short ball, it goes fine, and this one is almost over the keeper as he just gets a touch on it, Cummins' pace supplying the momentum. Last ball of the over? On the hip, glanced for four.
The ton is up in the 23rd over. Australia are being flayed.
21st over: South Africa 90-0 (Markram 38, Ackerman 51) Short, pulled, fine, single, that's the Ackerman formula today, and he repeats it to raise his fifty. Showed some good signs through a difficult evening of batting in Gqeberha, then got himself out the next morning. Today he's been given a much easier forum in which to show his skills.
Markram on strike, then, and he utterly flays Hazlewood! That is a shot of supreme confidence, and total dominance. A huge stride outside the off stump, a ball on a Hazlewood length heading towards the top of its bounce, and Markram with an angled bat smokes that ball, on the up. You couldn't really call it a cover drive, with the bat so far from body at the point of contact. Imagine one of those Brendon McCullum flat-bats over cover, but one designed by a fine filigree jeweller. Astonishing.
Never Gonna Give You Up comes onto the PA. Australia have been Rickrolled today.
20th over: South Africa 83-0 (Markram 33, Ackerman 49) Cummins to Ackerman around the wicket, trying a couple of shorties, but the second of those doesn't get up, and Ackerman pulls it comfortably to fine leg for one.
19th over: South Africa 82-0 (Markram 33, Ackerman 48) A maiden over! What is this sorcery! Not because Hazlewood bowled anything particularly unplayable, but I would guess more than Markram has assessed their incredible early position and wants to make sure he stabilises it.
Matthew Doherty emails succinctly. "Edgbaston 2005, England 409 all out, 80 overs first day."
That does rather spring to mind, doesn't it? Likewise, Australia 364 for 2 in Brisbane, 2002.
18th over: South Africa 82-0 (Markram 33, Ackerman 48) Reverse sweep from Ackerman! He's flying now. Takes a chance to disrupt Lyon, who is bowling around the wicket to the left-hander. Lyon is in the team for experience and guile, and needs to tap into those qualities. Ackerman takes him through the leg side for a couple more runs, then punches in front of point for four!
This. Is. A. Pasting.
Going at 4.5 an over through the first session of the Test, after being asked to bat.
17th over: South Africa 72-0 (Markram 33, Ackerman 38) Finally Hazlewood manages to apply the brakes for a couple of minutes. A dinky little pull shot from Ackerman gets a run to fine leg, with some risk. Even in a good over, Hazlewood's line strays there. One other single to Markram.
new_text:
Starc finishes with figures of 16.3-2-72-6. Even by the standards of South Africa v Australia, that was a blistering, tumultous day's play between the two best teams in the world. Conveniently, it breaks into four parts.
WICKET! South Africa 329 all out (Rabada LBW b Starc 0)
Mitchell Starc is a champion. You knew this, but my goodness this is some spell of bowling. Rabada is trapped in front by another beautiful full-length delivery, this one swinging away from the left-hander to smash the pad in front of middle and leg. Starc has obliterated the lower order with the second new ball, taking four wickets for no runs in six deliveries.
"I'm just brainstorming here," says Paul O'Neill, "but do you think a series like this could run to five Tests at some stage in the future?"
Mate, why don't you bugger off to TikTok? (Actually, here's a question - if you could pick one SA v Aus series to go to five Tests, what would it be? My first thought is the second series in 1993-94, given how close and crotchety those series were.)
Five wickets for Starc! A big inswinger hits Gerald Coetzee on the pad and ricochets onto the stumps. This is sensational clutch bowling from Starc, who is on a hat-trick after striking with the last ball of his previous over. What a day of Test cricket!
82nd over: South Africa 329-8 (Harmer 0, Coetzee 0) Cummins, hunting his first Test wicket in 50 overs, shares the new ball. Nothing happens in that over, but...
81st over: South Africa 328-8 (Harmer 0, Coetzee 0) That's so good from Mitchell Starc. It's one thing to take two wickets in an over; it's another to take out both set batters in the first over with the second new ball.
Pick that out! Jansen is bowled by a gorgeous inswinging yorker from Starc, who has taken two wickets in an over for the second time today. It curved in to smooch the bottom of off stump as Jansen tried to jab his bat down. He played beautifully but had almost no chance with that.
WICKET! South Africa 327-7 (Rickelton LBW b Starc 42)
Another lurch on this topsy-turvy day of Test cricket. Rickelton is undressed by a full delivery from Starc hat swings late to trap him plumb in front. He tried to clip it to leg, missed by a mile and didn't even discuss a review with Marco Jansen. That's the end of a quietly vital innings.
80th over: South Africa 325-6 (Rickelton 41, Jansen 51) After another accurate over from Nathan Lyon, and with just under half an hour remaining, the new ball is available. Mitchell Starc will take it.
79th over: South Africa 324-6 (Rickelton 40, Jansen 51) Jansen pushes Connolly sensibly to long on for a single before turning a couple past fine leg later in the over. His ball-striking has always been spectacular, but today he has looked like a batter who is starting to realise just how good he could be.
And the ball-striking is still spectacular. He carts a long hop from Connolly over midwicket for four to reach a fabulous fifty from 66 balls. He's leading from No8.
78th over: South Africa 315-6 (Rickelton 38, Jansen 44) Lyon rests on his haunches when Jansen thick-edges a defensive stroke to safety on leg side. Lyon has been good today: 22-1-70-2.
76th over: South Africa 308-6 (Rickelton 35, Jansen 40) "Cummins may be trying to vary the batters' expectations with such frequent changes, much as a bowler likes to vary each ball of an over," says John Starbuck. "He's thinking like a bowler-captain although in not allowing the batters to settle, he isn't allowing his bowlers either."
75th over: South Africa 306-6 (Rickelton 34, Jansen 39) Four from Connolly's over. Australia are trying to get to the new ball as quickly as possible. They should get 20-25 minutes with it tonight.
73rd over: South Africa 302-6 (Rickelton 33, Jansen 36) Connolly switches ends to replace Hazlewood. Has Pat Cummins always made this many bowling changes or has it developed over time? It seems a lot, even to an ADHDer.
The impassive Jansen clouts a full ball through midwicket for four to bring up South Africa's 300. He is some player, surely the best Test allrounder in the world.
72nd over: South Africa 297-6 (Rickelton 32, Jansen 32) Pat Cummins loves a bowling change; the latest is Matt Renshaw for Cooper Connolly. Renshaw's second ball is a full toss that Rickelton drives lazily through mid-on for four.
"I'm interested to see how Rickelton does here," writes Eddy Nason. "He was one of the standouts in the Hundred (so kill me, I only have access to so much cricket highlights in Canada), and it would be great fun to see him teeing off against the Aussies."
So far he's played an anti-Hundred innings, sensible to the point of being old-fashioned. In red-ball cricket he looks a lot more comfortable at No6.
71st over: South Africa 292-6 (Rickelton 27, Jansen 32) After 20 Tests, Marco Jansen averaged a handy 20.42 with the bat. Four games later his average is pushing 27 after a fine run of scores, all against India or Australia: 93, 26, 35, 85, 32*.
A quiet over from Hazlewood. There's just under an hour's play remaining, so Australia will get their hands on the second new ball before the close.
70th over: South Africa 291-6 (Rickelton 26, Jansen 32) Lyon off, Connolly on. His third ball, well wide of Rickelton's off stump, doesn't bounce at all and nutmegs Carey before scooting away for four byes. That's not a great sight on day one, especially if you chose to bowl first.
69th over: South Africa 285-6 (Rickelton 25, Jansen 31) Jansen lashes through the covers for four, not once but twice. Few, if any, lower-order batters in world cricket hit the ball so cleanly. The second boundary brings up a calm counter-attacking fifty partnership with Rickelton.
68th over: South Africa 276-6 (Rickelton 25, Jansen 22) South Africa are so good at scoring lower-order runs. Since their return to Test cricket in 1992, they average 93 for the last four wickets - the highest of any team bar Ireland, whose sample size is small.
A couple of singles take this particular seventh-wicket partnership to 44. That may not seem a lot but it's worth plenty after South Africa collapsed from 203/1 to 232/6.
67th over: South Africa 273-6 (Rickelton 23, Jansen 21) Hazlewood does come in, but his first ball is a touch wide and Rickelton cuts it sweetly for four. Apparently Cummins, who was replaced by Hazlewood, has bowled almost 50 overs since his last wicket - the longest drought of his Test career. Time for drinks.
"I'm already getting queasy premonitions of Marco Jansen's first Test hundred in December after coming in at 120-6 and swatting England's bumper theory to all parts while a bemused Joe Root shakes his head sadly," says Phil Harrison. "He's that kind of player."
He is, and that's not mean pejoratively. He would walk into a world Test XI.
66th over: South Africa 269-6 (Rickelton 19, Jansen 21) A full back from Lyon is flicked crisply through midwicket for four by Rickelton, who is playing a responsible innings. It might be worth Australia going back to Hazlewood, who sorted Rickelton out with the minimum of fuss in the first Test.
65th over: South Africa 262-6 (Rickelton 13, Jansen 20) Cummins tries some rough stuff from around the wicket. Jansen takes it on and belts a terrific pull through midwicket for four. He has skipped to 20 from 25 balls and is again proving a problem for Australia.
64th over: South Africa 256-6 (Rickelton 13, Jansen 14) Jansen waves Lyon to long on for a single. Rickelton is the senior batter but Jansen, who can be so dangerous, feels like the big wicket.
Lyon yells in vain for LBW when Rickelton offers no stroke to a ball round round the wicket. Missing off.
63rd over: South Africa 255-6 (Rickelton 13, Jansen 13) Cummins has changed ends to replace Starc. The lights have been switched on, which is never bad news for a quick bowler. Rickelton misses a loose hook stroke before clattering a boundary between extra cover and mid-off. Nicely played.
Rickelton is not out! There was an inside edge so Rickelton survives. An excellent decision from Richard Kettleborough, who is umpiring his 100th Test.
Australia review for LBW against Rickelton! Nathan Lyon comes on for Pat Cummins. Rickelton touches a loose ball past short fine leg for his first boundary - but then there's a big shout for LBW when Rickelton plays defensively down the wrong line. This looks exceedingly close.
61st over: South Africa 245-6 (Rickelton 5, Jansen 11) "This is a funny old series and no mistake," writes Felix Wood. "Is that three SA batters out hooking and one to a rookie part-time spinner? That seems careless to say the least."
60.3 overs: South Africa 244-6 (Rickelton 5, Jansen 10) Jansen stands tall to larrup Starc square on the off side for four. Later in the over, Rickelton takes a painful blow on the bottom hand as he tries to ride a lifter. It has drawn blood and there's a break in play while he receives treatment.
60th over: South Africa 238-6 (Rickelton 4, Jansen 5) Australia continue to hammer the middle of the pitch, and Jansen cuts a short ball from Cummins through backward point for his first boundary. The game and series are deliciously poised after a remarkable fightback from Australia, who were in all sorts at 203 for 1.
59th over: South Africa 233-6 (Rickelton 4, Jansen 1) Marco Jansen is a dangerous player, but Australia will fancy their chances of tempting him into something injudicious. He edges a back-foot drive through the vacant slip cordon for a single - Australia have nobody catching behind the wicket apart from Carey.
58th over: South Africa 232-6 (Rickelton 4, Jansen 0) Pace from both ends now, with Cummins replacing Connolly. He also rams everything in short, with the field set accordingly, and it's a maiden to Rickelton.
57th over: South Africa 232-6 (Rickelton 4, Jansen 0) Starc didn't realise Mulder had top-edged that hook. But he did and Starc has bowled a double-wicket maiden.
As good as Australia have been, South Africa's batting has left an abundancy to be desired.
WICKET! South Africa 232-6 (Mulder c Carey b Starc 0)
Australia are rampant! Mulder top-edges a hook through to Carey and is on his way for a two-ball duck. South Africa have lost five for 29 in 12.1 overs, and now, almost unbelievably, Australia are on top.
WICKET! South Africa 232-5 (Bedingham c Hazlewood b Starc 50)
That's why David Bedingham has a Test average of 36. He has given his wicket away and Australia are right back in the game. Bedingham, who was hit in the breadbasket by the previous delivery from Starc, top-edged a hook that was outstandingly caught by Hazlewood on the fine leg boundary. He took the catch just inside the toblerone, threw the ball up before he fell backwards and then jumped back onto the field to complete the catch.
56th over: South Africa 232-4 (Bedingham 50, Rickelton 4) Madon, that's a jaffa from Connolly. It curved onto middle stump, spat past Bedingham's defensive stroke and missed the off stump by a whisker.
Bedingham responds with a back cut for three to bring a high-class fifty, his fifth in Tests, from 78 balls. His Test average of 36 is a bald-faced lie; he's a terrific batter.
55th over: South Africa 228-4 (Bedingham 47, Rickelton 3) Mitchell Starc starts a new spell with no slips and an imaginary target halfway down the pitch. Bedingham pulls smoothly for a single. There's a more orthodox field for Rickelton, who cuts a single of his own to deep point.
"Deeply Dippy?" sniffs Roland Marshall. "Damn you, Smyth! I'd just about forgotten about the existence of that filth, but you just had to bring it back front and centre."
Which is where it should be. For some poor souls, that song was a rite of passage.
54th over: South Africa 226-4 (Bedingham 46, Rickelton 2) Connolly continues after tea, with Labuschagne at slip providing the soundtrack. He oohs and aahs after every delivery, even when Bedingham sweeps firmly behind square for four.Bedingham looks such a good player, and this would be a helluva day to convert one of his many starts. He has reached 30 on 15 occasions in Tests but has only one century.
"My recollection of that Richards innings at Durban in 1970 is that Ali Bacher ran himself out in the last over before lunch trying to get Barry on strike so he could go for it," writes Nick Robb. "It was Barry's second Test, not his first which was what Mark Nicholas said on commentary. With Bacher gone, Richards and Pollock proceeded to put on 102 in the first hour after lunch, Barry then departing for 140. Ian Chappell said to Stackpole during their partnership 'Now we're in real trouble - whatever Richards makes, that bastard will double.' He was wrong: Graeme fell short after making 274."
The evening session David Beginham, Ryan Rickelton and 11 Australian gentlemen walk out after tea. Big session, this, one that could decide the series.
